# Regulating the advertising of unhealthy foods is a priority action to prevent childhood and adolescent obesity.

**This is established in the executive report “Exploratory research for Colombia on the promotion and advertising of unhealthy foods and beverages aimed at children and adolescents”, prepared by the Marketing Studies group of EAFIT University for Unicef, Colombia, which published a summary, in comic format, in the magazine** [**Descubre y Crea**](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/publicaciones/descubre-y-crea) **.**

**Through the analysis of regulatory frameworks and fieldwork in six municipalities of the country with high rates of early childhood obesity, it was concluded that it is necessary to strengthen public policies and regulations in traditional and digital media, due to the emotional impact that advertising content generates in children.**

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [Our Impact](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/nuestro-impacto)
- Regulating the Advertising of Unhealthy Foods: A Priority Action to Prevent Childhood and Adolescent Obesity

![Imagen Regular la publicidad de alimentos no saludables, una acción prioritaria para prevenir la obesidad infantil y juvenil](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/b5bcf312-a26a-4561-8161-60da7731509b/web/Rombo-misalud.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=Y7mewAFP)

Since 2002, the WHO has highlighted the importance of regulating the advertising of food and beverages aimed at children and adolescents.

In Colombia, childhood obesity is a growing concern. According to the latest National Nutritional Status Survey (ENSIN), 24.4% of children are overweight, and 17.7% of adolescents are at risk of obesity. A recent study led by the Marketing Studies group at EAFIT University for UNICEF explored how advertising for unhealthy foods and beverages, such as ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks, influences the consumption choices of Colombian children and adolescents.

For the development of the study, international regulatory frameworks and standards were analyzed, in addition to fieldwork conducted with a sample of 111 students and 19 caregivers and teachers in educational institutions in six municipalities across the country with high rates of childhood obesity. Laura Isabel Rojas De Francisco, professor at the EAFIT School of Management and coordinator of the Marketing Studies group, emphasizes that the research provides key evidence to strengthen policies and regulations on the advertising of unhealthy foods and beverages that reach children and adolescents through various media.

“Advertising can contain content that evokes social connections, feelings, and representations, such as the relationship with family or friends enjoying different products, projecting images of well-being and closeness that generate recall and are popular among peers. This leads to emotional purchasing decisions,” says Professor Laura.

Although laws such as Law 1355 of 2009 and Resolution 810 of 2021 exist, regulatory gaps persist that allow brands to reach minors without effective control, especially in the digital environment. This is compounded by a lack of awareness of the regulations and a disconnect between different stakeholders, which can result in fragmented monitoring and control processes, or the perception of excessive regulation.

“While there has been progress in traditional media, there is still much to be done in the digital environment, especially on social media and gaming platforms,” adds Professor Laura, noting that the advertising most remembered by children is found on television and YouTube, where challenges _and calls to action_ are presented that encourage them to try foods and drinks that can have negative health effects. According to Lina Patricia Zapata Vélez, Health and Nutrition Officer at UNICEF Colombia, 80% of the leading food and beverage companies operate in the sector with products high in fat, salt, or sugar, and 22.6% of brands pay for exposure on online gaming platforms. Therefore, it is a priority to define a common agenda that allows for the creation of a regulatory framework for its proper regulation.

The children and adolescents who participated in the research also remember the advertising they saw in stores and on product packaging. This exposure, combined with the taste experience and the visual impact of what they see in different media, significantly influences their consumption decisions, often with major consequences for their health. Overweight and obesity are largely due to "obesogenic environments," that is, spaces that promote the consumption of high-calorie foods and physical inactivity, explains Lina. These conditions "reduce the life expectancy and quality of life of children, adolescents, and pregnant women in Colombia, due to associated diseases such as high blood pressure, diabetes, and depression from an early age, and premature deaths from these causes."

Laura Sierra Zapata, a professor at the School of Applied Sciences and Engineering at EAFIT, adds that during childhood and adolescence, the gut microbiota is still developing. Therefore, at this stage, “foods low in nutrients and high in simple starches should be avoided, and replaced with those that, even if fortified, provide nutrients as well as calories. It is recommended to avoid sugary drinks and to instill eating and lifestyle habits that are in harmony with our biology, which is similar to the health that any ecosystem needs.”

###### Key actions for improved child food health

With the aim of creating healthier food environments and protecting future generations from the effects of advertising that promotes harmful eating habits, the research proposes rethinking the self-regulation model in the food industry and conducting rigorous audits of digital platforms to ensure data protection. It also suggests setting limits on the creation of challenges that encourage the consumption of unhealthy products. Regarding educational initiatives, the study emphasizes the importance of promoting programs that address food health and responsible consumption from childhood, involving social agents and opinion leaders to raise awareness about the link between childhood obesity and the influence of advertising. Furthermore, the creation of stricter policies regulating advertising in school and sports environments is considered necessary, following WHO guidelines and strengthening existing regulations. The findings of this research, notes Lina Patricia Zapata, have provided UNICEF Colombia with evidence to guide intersectoral and sustainable preventive actions that recognize children's rights to grow up in an environment that guarantees their healthy development. Furthermore, they have facilitated the promotion of technical cooperation processes to strengthen regulations on food advertising aimed at children and adolescents, as well as the improvement of public health interventions through accurate information for better decision-making.

Finally, Professor Laura Sierra recommends that families include at least three different types of fruit in the diets of children and adolescents, aiming for a weekly goal of 30 different fruits and vegetables, introduced in a fun and engaging way. She also suggests increasing fiber intake through nuts and dried fruit, choosing healthy oils and fats like avocado and olive oil, and incorporating whole grains such as quinoa, brown rice, and barley, along with fermented foods like yogurt and sourdough bread. All of this will contribute to optimal gut health from an early age.

###### Viruses versus bacteria: PhageLife's proposal for the swine sector from EAFIT

En una granja porcina, una infección bacteriana puede poner en riesgo la salud de los animales y la productividad del negocio. Además, el problema se vuelve más complejo cuando las bacterias dejan de responder a los antibióticos que antes permitían combatirlas. Para explorar otra vía, la empresa [PhageLife](https://phagelife.co/) desarrolla soluciones personalizadas con bacteriófagos, virus naturales capaces de eliminar bacterias específicas.

metadata.description: ​​En Colombia, la obesidad infantil es una preocupación creciente. Según la última Encuesta Nacional de la Situación Nutricional (ENSIN), el 24.4 % de niñas y niños presentan exceso de peso y el 17.7 % de los adolescentes están en riesgo de obesidad. Una reciente investigación liderada por el grupo de Estudios en Mercadeo de EAFIT para UNICEF exploró cómo la publicidad de alimentos y bebidas no saludables, como los ultraprocesados y las bebidas azucaradas, influye en las decisiones de consumo de niñas, niños y adolescentes colombianos.
